SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule returns to Earth from the ISS

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (431 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth.
  • The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov.
  • According to recent reports, the freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth.

The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

According to recent reports, the freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT).

It has been revealed that the Dragon introduced Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

"Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.
  • It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.
  • Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.

It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

In a recent development, when Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he remarked: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me.".

In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message.

Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market.

For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

In a recent development, madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the blueprint is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

Recent findings suggest that where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

In a recent development, the idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

Who is Gabriel's newly introduced agent, Ali Barat?

"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat states he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

Sources indicate that his major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

"I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world.".

Industry observers note that this was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

It has been revealed that what makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

In a recent development, this included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, notes he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

He is an unashamed self-publicist, too.

"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

The largely AI-generated video which unveiled Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

Gabriel's deal is part of a new venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

"It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source mentioned. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family.".

Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

It is this newly introduced focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

The big question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

Sources indicate that by the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carla Ward has been in charge of the Republic of Ireland since 2025.

Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward has signed a contract extension until the conclusion of the side's Euro 2029 campaign.

The 42-year-old's previous deal was due to expire at the end of this World Cup qualification cycle but her future has now been resolved before next month's two-legged play-off final against Poland.

Ward replaced Eileen Gleeson at the helm in January 2025 and has led the side to promotion to League A in the Nations League and a highest ever position of 21st in the Fifa rankings.

The Republic of Ireland are just 180 minutes from next summer's World Cup in Brazil, with the first leg against Poland in Gdansk on 1 December before the reverse fixture four days later at Aviva Stadium.

"From the moment I arrived, I've felt a strong connection with this country, the players, the staff and, most importantly, the people. The way I've been welcomed and embraced has meant a huge amount to me, and it's a real privilege to lead this team and this nation," stated Ward.

"I'm incredibly proud of what we've achieved together so far, but what excites me most is what lies ahead. There's something really special about this group, their togetherness, their character and their willingness to fight for each other and for the jersey.

"I've always mentioned I want to build something that people can connect with, a team that reflects the spirit of this country, that people are proud of and genuinely feel part of. We've had some brilliant moments already, but I really believe we're only just getting started.".

Two down, two to go - Irish target back-to-back World Cups.

Mustaki out of World Cup play-off with knee injury.

Ward previously managed Sheffield United, Aston Villa and Birmingham City after a successful playing career during which she scored over 100 goals for Sheffield FC.

Since she became boss, the Republic of Ireland have won 12 of their 19 games and lost just one of their Nations League fixtures last year with the sole reverse coming away to Slovenia.

Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive officer David Courell stated Ward has helped give "women and girls' football around the country the platform it deserves" during her tenure.

"We are delighted to reach agreement with Carla to continue to lead our Ireland women's national team for the long term," he added.

"The energy that she has brought to the role has propelled the team towards, hopefully, qualifying for a second Fifa Women's World Cup and, in turn, giving women and girls' football around the country the platform it deserves.

"Extending Carla's contract demonstrates our ambition to keep moving forward, hopefully to the World Cup in Brazil and beyond to the Uefa European Championships in Germany in 2029.".

The Republic of Ireland are aiming to secure a spot at their second successive World Cup, while Poland have never qualified for the tournament before.

Ward's side defeated Kazakhstan in comfortable fashion in their play-off semi-final with Poland coming through a penalty shootout against Belgium.

Republic of Ireland must do without key defender Chloe Mustaki who has been forced to withdraw from the panel after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity.
  • Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image indicates the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.
  • In a recent development, the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like.

Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image indicates the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.

In a recent development, the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky.

"It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email.

In a recent development, lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an crucial step in the scientific process.".

This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data.

That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein.

It has been revealed that einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature.

The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became known as the event horizon of a black hole. The singularity, its heart. Black holes were born in 1915, decades before their discovery and over a century before the EHT saw one.

General relativity also predicted what the region around the event horizon would look like. A ring of superheated glowing plasma with the shadow of the black hole falling on it.When scientists first saw the image of M87* they were astounded at how close it reflected predictions made by general relativity, thus confirming the the theory once again. This verification further solidifies that development.

Verifying the EHT's image of M87* could lead to the CSIRO-developed technique being applied to some more "down-to-Earth" uses such as improving medical imaging and mapping earthquakes.

Recent findings suggest that "Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process, and it is especially valuable for results as novel as those of the EHT. It is extremely gratifying to see that GenDIReCT, an elegant, entirely independent method, recovers the ring structure of M87* across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration’s published results," Laurent Loinard, Director of the EHT Collaboration, remarked.

"Studies like this strengthen our confidence in what we have learned about black holes, and enrich the toolkit available to the whole community.".

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, Fresh Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

Novo indicates Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
  • Recent findings suggest that wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo.
  • When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Recent findings suggest that wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

According to recent reports, the detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," noted Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

In a recent development, while Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are at the moment no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

According to recent reports, but more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.

Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she remarked, pointing to the potential of future research.

‘The worst COP ever’ offers a chance to learn from failure

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protesters on the final day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey.
  • In a recent development, ‘The worst COP ever’ is how some people have described the United Nations COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, which ended on 22 November.
  • The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protesters on the final day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: Chris McGrath/Getty.

In a recent development, ‘The worst COP ever’ is how some people have described the United Nations COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, which ended on 22 November. COP31 was the first to take place after the confirmation that global warming will overshoot the safe limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. Despite a two-day extension to the meeting and several proposals for an overarching political declaration or ‘cover decision’, delegates left after two weeks of talks without such an agreement.

The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?

The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?

Drafted by the host nations (Turkey and Australia, this year), a cover decision is a statement that all countries can agree on at the end of the talks. It is not a legally binding text and is a relatively recent innovation. That participants failed to agree such a statement is not a surprise. It requires a willingness for give and take, which was in short supply because many of the countries that attended this year are at war, subject to economic and other sanctions, or involved in trade disputes. Furthermore, the United States, the world’s biggest economy and the largest historic carbon emitter, did not attend following its withdrawal from the COP process.

Delegates from the world’s poorest countries were angry that there was no mention of concrete measures to increase finance for climate adaptation — money that they will need to help them to become more resilient to climate shocks. Many delegates were also angry that the draft text did not include any reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels. Previous cover decisions have included such language, overcoming objections from fossil-fuel-producing states. This time, however, delegates from these states were more determined to block such wording.

Industry observers note that but there are key reasons why it would be wrong to conclude that such climate conferences have outlived their purpose — or that a consensus-based approach should be abandoned, as some have argued. There is always room to improve, but COP meetings are much more than what happens in the final days when high-level political representatives turn up.

Environmental treaties are paralysed — here’s how we can do better.

Environmental treaties are paralysed — here’s how we can do better.

Industry observers note that first, these meetings mainly involve discussions between technical experts and observers — including many researchers — representing the countries that have signed up to the UN’s climate agreement, known as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. For most of the two weeks (and in many timetabled talks before a COP), delegates meet in working groups to discuss a spectrum of climate-change topics. The Antalya meeting discussions included how to accelerate electrification, cut methane emissions and mobilize fresh finance to protect the world’s forests. Progress in these technical talks is often incremental. In contrast to the final days of a COP, which are organized around negotiations between political representatives, expert delegates focus on getting things done rather than posturing.

According to recent reports, the second reason not to write off this COP is that it’s not uncommon for countries to leave meetings without a high-level agreement. Indeed, some previous ‘good’ outcomes needed earlier COP meetings to ‘fail’. The landmark COP21 Paris climate agreement signed in 2015, a legally binding text in which nations agreed to limit global warming to 1.5 °C, is perhaps the best-known example. In 2009, COP15 in Copenhagen resulted in deadlock. That failure prompted deeper thinking and discussions at subsequent COP meetings on the steps needed for the world to stay within safe climate limits, laying the groundwork for the Paris agreement.

Sources indicate that still, the current geopolitical climate is a substantial obstacle to progress, affecting not only COP climate meetings but also talks on other international agreements, such as a proposed treaty to end plastic pollution. Another set of talks occurring at the same time as COP31 — on setting international restrictions on autonomous weapons — also failed to reach an agreement and will resume in 2028.

In a recent development, in the case of both the climate and plastics talks, a relatively small group of countries — including Iran, Russia and Saudi Arabia, which are heavily reliant on fossil-fuel exports, among others — are blocking stronger action. Some researchers, as well as country delegates, say that the UN’s method of decision-making (that all countries must agree a consensus) is the problem, and question whether there should instead be a vote and a decision made by majority.

Trust and science: the essential elements missing from plastics treaty talks.

Trust and science: the essential elements missing from plastics treaty talks.

It has been revealed that there is some logic in changing the approach for the cover decisions to avoid the overtly self-interested blocking of action. But for many other decisions made at UN climate and other environment-related meetings, abandoning a consensus-based approach in favour of a vote would not be a good option.

Sources indicate that the UN’s expert groups for example, including the scientists who are part of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (which synthesizes studies to inform decisions), must continue to work through consensus. Delegates painstakingly review, debate and discuss evidence, before coming to a conclusion — and it is crucial that all those involved are brought in at this point.

A change to voting might, in some cases, mean faster results, but it would also undermine the principles that everyone owns the result and that global problems need global solutions.

It has been revealed that it is right that, on reflecting on the COP in Antalya, many will ask what needs to change. And some aspects must. But altering how decisions are made should not be taken lightly. Climate change doesn’t respect borders. It won’t be solved by countries working on their own or in small groups.

Raya was helped off the pitch in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle on Saturday.

He hurt his left shoulder while claiming a cross and making contact with Newcastle forward William Osula.

"We need some more tests [on Tuesday] but it is quite encouraging," mentioned Gunners boss Arteta.

"With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action we were all quite worried but it seems to be better than what we expected," said Arteta.

"When you look at the action it doesn't seem to be much but the extent of the pain that he had and how he was struggling, it was quite worrying.

"We expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain he had in that moment.

It has been revealed that "The first tests that we have done have shown something that is much more encouraging. He does not need to have surgery which was the worry as that would rule him out for months so let's see.".

Raya set to have scan on injury - how much would Arsenal miss him?

And Raya is huge part of the way that Arsenal play because of his ability with the ball at his feet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They mentioned that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages.".

Police stated they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they mentioned.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also noted they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

  • LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.
  • Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.
  • Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese stated. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

It has been revealed that “So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

Industry observers note that “And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”.

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship.

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark remarked to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

It has been revealed that “Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese remarked. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”.

After the Championship game, Clark herself mentioned she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

Industry observers note that “But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”.

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

According to recent reports, “People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

According to recent reports, former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any challenges with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”.

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”.

#173824. England, Northern Ireland, Scotland & Wales to host 2035 Women's World Cup

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (998 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland & Wales to host 2035 Women's World Cup

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.
  • It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.
  • The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup.

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government revealed a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir.

Fifa announces UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup.

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, remarked: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations.".

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed latest Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium.

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, stated: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

"In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt.".

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come.".

In a recent development, fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation noted: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding concerns.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Edward Iordanescu's most recent job was with Legia Warsaw, who he left in October 2025.

Watford are set to appoint Edward Iordanescu as their new manager.

BBC Three Counties Radio report the Romanian is due to become the Hornets' sixth manager inside 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United in his 18th game in charge.

The 48-year-old is understood to be arriving in the UK on Tuesday to sign his contract and plans to bring three members of staff with him and hopes to be in the dugout for Wednesday's Championship fixture at home to Blackburn Rovers (19:45 GMT).

Iordanescu guided Romania at Euro 2024 where they topped their group ahead of Belgium with all four sides ending level on four points from three games before a 3-0 defeat against the Netherlands in the Round of 16.

Iordanescu - whose father Anghel had three spells in charge of the Romanian national team, leading them in two World Cups and two European Championships - left his last role at Polish club Legia Warsaw in October 2025.

It was the 48-year-old's ninth club over a 15-year coaching career which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj among others in his homeland.

Dionisi, who departed with the Hornets in 21st, four points above the relegation zone, was only appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

The 46-year-old Italian was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Glentoran manager Duncan Ferguson has been suspended for seven games following his red card in the side's 3-2 defeat by Cliftonville last week.
  • The former Everton striker was dismissed for how he addressed match officials after believing the Reds' opener at Solitude should have been ruled out for a foul in the build-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Duncan Ferguson jointly holds the record for the most red cards in Premier League history with eight.

Glentoran manager Duncan Ferguson has been suspended for seven games following his red card in the side's 3-2 defeat by Cliftonville last week.

The former Everton striker was dismissed for how he addressed match officials after believing the Reds' opener at Solitude should have been ruled out for a foul in the build-up.

The 1995 FA Cup winner arrived at the Oval in October and has so far won one, drawn two and lost one of his four games in charge.

"I want to apologise to the match officials for my behaviour on Friday night," noted the former Forest Green Rovers and Inverness Caledonian Thistle boss.

"I was frustrated by what happened on the pitch and let my emotions get the better of me. I went too far in the way I expressed that frustration towards the officials, and I should have handled the situation better.".

"I accept the suspension and I'll learn from what happened. My focus now is on the players, the staff and the work we've got to do together, both on and off the pitch.".

The sanction will start with Tuesday night's hosting of Larne in the Bet McLean Cup, a competition in which the east Belfast outfit have been beaten finalists the past two seasons.

Even should the Glens progress to the quarter-finals of the competition expected to take place next month, Ferguson's ban would still include the eagerly anticipated Boxing Day visit from fierce rivals Linfield.

  • 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STARBASE, Texas  — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless.

The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies.

For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity.

We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us.

It has been revealed that inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener.

Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close).

It has been revealed that fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how substantial the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare.

Starbase, Texas https://t.co/NqDWwUZXv9August 25, 2025.

In a recent development, as our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander.

Sources indicate that NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead.

But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials said the company is presently completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer's Starlink network in low Earth orbit at the moment consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were launched on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX looks to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the tech giant hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized.

It has been revealed that spaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on.

Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete.

Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy company began in the 1940s.

Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by.

It has been revealed that both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is at the moment constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets.

Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket releases and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction.

Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower.

That felt like science fiction too.

Recent findings suggest that josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.
  • It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the problem that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to enhancement copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the problem that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to enhancement copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Industry observers note that hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

Recent findings suggest that over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

In a recent development, "We slept here," noted Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from Newly introduced York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She mentioned they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

According to recent reports, justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz remarked she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

Industry observers note that "It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she stated.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Recent findings suggest that officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy noted Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

According to recent reports, "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump stated Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

In a recent development, shortly after the ground stop, Duffy said he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

"Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," mentioned Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
  • After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".
  • Sources indicate that "I understand that there is no agreement on this text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".

Sources indicate that "I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," noted Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

In a recent development, around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

According to recent reports, the deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

It has been revealed that and so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good.".

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Sources indicate that countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, noted in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

In a recent development, it's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

Industry observers note that but ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and promptly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," mentioned UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.
  • The club’s latest ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.
  • More than $600 million was spent on bringing massive-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s latest ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing massive-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on latest signings. Here's why that's significant.

But, on Sunday, the club unveiled that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s initiative for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali remarked in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”.

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected newly introduced signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls presently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel.

“Todd [Boehly] noted he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”.

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.
  • Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.
  • Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4QNovember 17, 2026.

From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson mentioned in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.".

Sources indicate that pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our newly introduced James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.".

According to recent reports, in 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.
